title: Moffat County Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Moffat County wells have a 217-foot median depth and an 8 gpm median yield. See local drilling costs, water-level records and checks before buying.
h1: What to Expect From a Well in Moffat County
intro_html:
A well budget near Craig should not be carried over to a lot near Maybell or Dinosaur without checking local records. Moffat County has mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground, and reported well depths vary widely.

Colorado DWR records include 4,333 permitted wells across the county, with 2,518 recorded as constructed. The figures below cover all permitted uses, not just residential wells. They are a starting point for evaluating a property—not a prediction of what a new hole will produce.

sections.heading: A 217-Foot Median Leaves Plenty of Room for a Different Bid
sections.html:
Among the 2,625 wells reporting depth, the median is 217 feet. The middle half runs from 73 to 360 feet. For a buyer, that spread matters more than the midpoint alone: a bid based only on the median can miss a substantial amount of drilling. The 90th-percentile depth is 500 feet.

Mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground helps explain why nearby completion records matter. Aquifer labels are often broad: 4,130 permits fall under unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, compared with 63 Alluvial and 32 Wasatch-Fort Union wells. Those labels do not establish the exact geology beneath your parcel. Ask the driller which nearby logs best match your site.

sections.heading: Reported Yields Center on 8 GPM, Not Unlimited Ranch Water
sections.html:
The 521 wells with reported pump yields have a median of 8.0 gpm, with the middle half between 6.0 and 12.0 gpm. That suggests useful household supply is common among reporting wells, but a recorded pumping rate is not a guarantee of sustained delivery during heavy use.

Reported yields include 11% in the 1–5 gpm range and 70% in the 5–15 gpm range. The under-1-gpm share is 0%; that does not prove dry holes or poorly producing wells are absent. Before buying, get a current pumping and recovery test. Match the results to household demand, livestock needs and storage, and confirm that the permit authorizes the intended uses.

sections.heading: Moffat's Water-Level Records Do Not Show a Steady Decline
sections.html:
Static water level is the depth to standing water in a resting well, not the depth of the drilled hole. Across 205 reporting wells, the median is 77 feet below ground, and the middle half spans 31–140 feet. Pump selection also needs the water level while pumping, not just this resting measurement.

Decade medians are 80 feet in the 1980s, 65 in the 2000s, 82 in the 2010s and 64 in the 2020s. These figures fluctuate rather than showing steadily deeper water. They also represent different reporting wells, not continuous measurements at the same locations. They cannot establish that water levels on a particular Craig, Maybell or Dinosaur property are stable.

sections.heading: A Long Permit History, With Household and Stock Uses Leading
sections.html:
Moffat County's permit history extends from 6 permits in the 1950s to records as recent as 2026. The 1990s account for 820 permits, compared with 659 in the 2000s, 490 in the 2010s and 470 in the 2020s. The latest decade is incomplete, so those totals should not be read as a straight construction trend.

Domestic or household use accounts for 55% of records and stock use for 25%. Prominent driller entries include Craig Drilling (Herod, James Leroy), with 267 records, and Visintainer Co. (Visintainer, Walter), with 251. “Authorized (Pe, Pg)” appears on 348 records but is not a clear business name. Historical entries do not establish current availability or licensing.

sections.heading: Budget Beyond the Drilled Hole in Moffat County
sections.html:
The local cost model uses $50–$75 per foot for mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. At the 217-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole at about $10,800–$16,300. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at $16,800–$28,300.

Treat those figures as a planning range, not a site quote. The broad depth spread means the footage allowance deserves close attention. Ask what the bid includes for casing and grout, how additional drilling is priced, and where trenching and electrical allowances stop. Access preparation, septic work and the rest of the building site need separate scope discussions rather than being assumed part of the finished-well estimate.

sections.heading: Check Water Quality and Failure Risk Separately From Depth
sections.html:
The environmental screening inventory lists 68 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 33 historic mine features and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. These are screening flags, not proof that a particular well is contaminated. A PFAS sampling location does not by itself establish a detection or an unsafe household supply.

For an existing well, arrange laboratory testing and use nearby site information to discuss additional analytes with the laboratory or local health officials. Review casing, grout and drainage around the wellhead. Reported yield statistics do not provide a dry-hole rate. On a building lot, coordinate the well location with septic siting, required setbacks, construction access and protection from surface runoff.

sections.heading: Before Closing Near Craig, Maybell or Dinosaur
sections.html:
Start with the parcel's DWR permit, well completion report and pump records. Confirm that the well serving the property matches those documents and that its authorized uses fit your plans. A household-use permit should not be assumed to cover irrigation or livestock simply because neighboring properties have those uses.

Next, compare nearby constructed wells around Craig, Maybell or Dinosaur rather than relying only on the county median. Request a written drilling scope for vacant land, or a current pumping test and water-quality results for an existing home. Settle driveway access, well placement, septic feasibility and utility routing before fixing the house location. These checks turn countywide averages into a practical purchase or building decision.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Moffat County, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported depth is 217 feet, and the middle half of wells ranges from 73 to 360 feet. The 90th-percentile depth is 500 feet. These figures come from 2,625 depth reports across all permitted uses. For a specific lot, nearby completion logs are a better bidding reference than the county median alone.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Moffat County?
faq.a: The planning model uses $50–$75 per foot. At the county's 217-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $10,800–$16,300, while a finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $16,800–$28,300. Ask for a site-specific quote that spells out casing, grout, access requirements and charges if drilling goes deeper than expected.

faq.q: How much water does a Moffat County well produce?
faq.a: Among 521 reported pump yields, the median is 8.0 gpm and the middle half is 6.0–12.0 gpm. Reported yields include 11% in the 1–5 gpm range. A historical yield is not a current performance guarantee. Have the well tested for pumping and recovery, then evaluate supply against your intended demand and permitted uses.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Moffat County?
faq.a: County permit records cannot establish drinking-water safety. The environmental inventory lists 68 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 33 historic mine features and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Those listings do not prove contamination at your well. Get laboratory testing and review nearby environmental concerns before deciding which additional tests are appropriate.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Moffat County?
faq.a: The available decade medians do not show a steady decline. Depth to water was 80 feet in the 1980s, 65 in the 2000s, 82 in the 2010s and 64 in the 2020s. These are different groups of reporting wells, not repeated measurements of the same wells. Property-specific measurements are needed to assess a local trend.
